candidates.title: Verifier-guided vs. generator-only repair under simulated telemetry faults
candidates.research_question: Does integrating a deterministic validator with an LLM repair pipeline reduce unsafe-apply rates and regressions when telemetry is faulty (stale/missing/noisy) compared to an LLM-only repair pipeline?
hypotheses: H1: A verifier-guided LLM pipeline yields a lower unsafe-apply rate than LLM-only under all tested telemetry-fault conditions.
H2: The relative benefit of verifier guidance increases as telemetry corruption (staleness/missing fields/noise) increases.
H3: Some classes of regressions persist even with verifier guidance (e.g., semantic policy misinterpretation).
candidates.proposed_design: Build a controlled task bank of 120 intent->configuration repair tasks (multi-vendor syntactic templates) derived from public benchmarks and synthetic topologies. For each task create 3 telemetry-fault variants: stale, missing, noisy. Implement two pipelines: (A) LLM-only: generate repair and output config; (B) LLM+Validator: LLM proposes repair, deterministic validator (Batfish-style reachability/policy checks) verifies and rejects or requests repair; allow one automated repair iteration. Execute both pipelines across tasks and fault variants. Record raw outputs, validator traces, and labelled outcomes. Adhere to preregistered retry policy and seeds for orchestration; cap total model calls.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task raw LLM outputs, validator pass/fail traces, final applied-config candidate, binary unsafe-apply label (would violate reachability/policy), regression taxonomy labels, per-task latency and number of iterations. Aggregate counts by pipeline and telemetry-fault level.
candidates.primary_outcome: Reduction in unsafe-apply rate (percentage points) of LLM+Validator vs LLM-only, with 95% CI across tasks and fault conditions.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute per-task paired differences in unsafe-apply (binary) and regression counts; use McNemar's test or paired permutation test for unsafe-apply differences, bootstrap CIs for percent-reduction, subgroup analyses by fault type, and descriptive failure-mode taxonomy. Report exact p-values and effect sizes.
risks: Deterministic validator may be weaker than assumed (coverage gaps) causing false negatives/positives.
Synthetic task bank may not represent production heterogeneity; external validity limited.
Hosted model API rate limits or outages could force reruns within budget constraints.

candidates.title: Prompt framing and run stochasticity: paired vs isolated evaluation effects on NetOps outcomes
candidates.research_question: How sensitive are NetOps safety outcomes (unsafe-apply rate, regression rate) to prompt framing and LLM run-to-run stochasticity, and does a paired-evaluation design reduce apparent variance in comparative assessments?
hypotheses: H1: Prompt framing (instruction wording, examples) materially changes unsafe-apply and regression rates for the same tasks.

H2: Run-to-run stochasticity produces nontrivial variability; paired evaluation (same random seeds/ordering per task across conditions) reduces measured variance and Type I error in model comparisons.
H3: Some prompt variations produce systematic bias (e.g., aggressive 'apply' framing increases unsafe-apply rate).
candidates.proposed_design: Select 80 NetOps repair/change tasks. Define 6 prompt framings (neutral, conservative, aggressive, with example, without example, explicit-validator-instruction). For each task and framing, execute N=10 independent LLM runs (to capture stochasticity). Implement two evaluation designs: (1) isolated: compare aggregate metrics per framing; (2) paired: for each task, compare outputs across framings using matched-run indices. Measure unsafe-apply and regression labels via a deterministic validator. Pre-register prompt templates, run counts, and comparison tests.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task, per-framing sets of N LLM outputs, validator traces, binary unsafe-apply labels, regression counts, and per-run tokens/latency. Variance estimates within framing and paired differences across framings.
candidates.primary_outcome: Quantified prompt-framing effect sizes on unsafe-apply rate and reduction in variance/Type I error afforded by paired evaluation (e.g., change in standard error or p-value stability).
candidates.analysis_outline: Estimate within-framing variance (binomial proportion CI) and between-framing differences using paired McNemar/permutation tests; compute intraclass correlation and repeatability. Simulate false-positive rates under both isolated and paired analysis via resampling. Report sensitivity to number of runs N.
risks: High run counts increase model-call cost; must balance N within model-calls budget.
Deterministic-seed control is limited by hosted API stochasticity; pairing relies on matched ordering rather than true RNG seeding.
Prompt-space is large; chosen framings may not cover all practical operator styles.

candidates.title: A compact construct-validity rubric predicting execution-time safety
candidates.research_question: Can a compact, operational construct-validity rubric for NetOps tasks predict execution-time safety outcomes (unsafe-apply rate) measured by validators, and which rubric components are most predictive?
hypotheses: H1: A multi-component rubric (metrics: validator-coverage, task-complexity, telemetry-fidelity, action-criticality) will correlate significantly with observed unsafe-apply rates (negative correlation for higher rubric quality).
H2: Validator-coverage and telemetry-fidelity are the strongest single predictors of operational safety.
H3: The rubric enables prioritization (rank-order) of tasks for human review with better precision than naive heuristics (e.g., complexity alone).
candidates.proposed_design: Design a 4-component rubric with discrete scores per task (0–3 each): validator-coverage, task-complexity, telemetry-fidelity, action-criticality. Assemble a 100-task corpus (mix of repair/change tasks used in other candidates). For each task, collect LLM-generated repairs (one strong prompt) and validator outcomes to compute observed unsafe-apply rates. Independently score each task using the rubric by blinded annotators following clear rules (automated where possible). Correlate rubric scores and components with observed unsafe-apply rate and compute predictive metrics for prioritization.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task rubric component scores, aggregate rubric total scores, observed unsafe-apply rates from validator traces, and prioritization precision/recall curves for human-review triage at various thresholds.
candidates.primary_outcome: Correlation coefficient (Spearman rho) between rubric total score and observed unsafe-apply rate, plus component-wise predictive importance (e.g., via logistic regression coefficients).
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute Spearman/Pearson correlations, fit logistic regression for unsafe-apply~rubric components, cross-validated AUC for triage thresholds, and report bootstrapped CIs. Perform ablation to measure component contribution.
risks: Rubric scoring may require human judgment and introduce subjectivity; inter-annotator agreement must be measured.
Observed correlations may depend on the validator strength used; weak validators reduce signal.
Construct validity of rubric itself must be defended and may need iteration.

candidates.title: Adversarial prompt-injection against verifier-guided NetOps pipelines
candidates.research_question: Can targeted adversarial prompts or crafted corner-case inputs induce unsafe configuration changes in LLM-generated NetOps outputs, and to what extent does a deterministic validator mitigate these adversarial successes?
hypotheses: H1: Carefully crafted adversarial prompts increase unsafe-apply rates for LLM-only pipelines compared to benign prompts.
H2: Deterministic validators reduce but do not eliminate adversarially induced unsafe applies; some adversarial cases exploit validator coverage gaps.
H3: Adversarial prompts have transferability across prompt templates and model seeds to a measurable degree.
candidates.proposed_design: Construct 60 adversarial prompt variants using automated perturbation strategies (e.g., addition of conflicting instructions, obfuscated constraints, incentive framing) and 60 matched benign prompts. For a set of 80 NetOps tasks, run each prompt variant under two pipelines: LLM-only and LLM+Validator (single verification iteration). Label unsafe-apply outcomes via an independent validator and analyze transferability by testing adversarial prompts across multiple prompt templates and multiple LLM runs.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task, per-prompt-label outputs, validator pass/fail traces, adversarial-success rate (increase in unsafe-apply vs benign), examples of adversarial patterns that evade validator, and transferability statistics across prompts and runs.
candidates.primary_outcome: Adversarial success rate (increase in unsafe-apply probability) for LLM-only and residual success rate after validator, with statistical comparison (e.g., risk ratio and CI).
candidates.analysis_outline: Compare adversarial vs benign unsafe-apply rates using paired tests, compute risk ratios with bootstrap CIs, analyze successful adversarial cases for common patterns and validator-coverage gaps, and test transferability by cross-applying adversarial prompts. Report exact counts and qualitative taxonomy of evasions.
risks: Generating realistic adversarial prompts may require iterative human-in-the-loop development during design (allowed pre-lock only); post-lock automated generation must be carefully constrained by preregistration.
Ethical concerns: must avoid publishing adversarial prompts that enable harmful misuse—redact or abstract attack patterns in final outputs if necessary.
Adversarial effects may be model-specific; transferability may be limited, constraining generality.
